- If sentiment is consistently positive (≥ 0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate; reduce forecast slightly, especially after sharp spikes.
- If sentiment is consistently negative (≤ -0.33), model tends to underestimate; increase forecast slightly, especially if recent price is falling.
- After a strong upward spike (e.g., >85), model often overshoots and fails to correct; cap forecast at +5–10% below peak or adjust downward if sentiment turns negative.
- If model shows steady upward trend with no sentiment reversal, check for mean reversion — true price often pulls back after 3–5 days of rising forecast.
- When sentiment shifts from positive to negative mid-period, model often lags; adjust forecast downward by 2–5% for next 3–5 days if sentiment drops below 0.33.
- If model forecast is flat or rising slowly while sentiment is volatile, consider short-term mean reversion — true price may dip within 3–7 days.
- For 30-day horizon, if model is consistently above 90 and sentiment is weak or negative, reduce forecast by 5–10% to avoid overconfidence bias.
- If true price drops sharply after model peak, consider sentiment-driven “panic” correction — model may not capture sudden negative sentiment momentum.
